newsitem.title: HAITI: Cheering crowds greet former Haiti police chief.
newsitem.headline: Cheering crowds greet former Haiti police chief.

text.p: Cheering crowds greeted former police chief Dany Toussaint on his return to Haiti on Wednesday after two months in detention in Miami for questioning by U.S. officials about political killings.
"They asked me questions which I couldn't answer about the deaths of some people," Toussaint told reporters on arrival at Port-au-Prince airport. "I'm happy I'm back."

A crowd of people cheered and chanted his name as he emerged from the airport. When he arrived on Jan. 22 at Miami International Airport, he was held by immigration officials who questioned the validity of his Green Card work permit.

He was later questioned by Federal Bureau of Investigation officials about his relationship with former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide and about the March 1995 assassination of military spokeswoman Mireille Durocher-Bertin.

The U.S. Embassy and the FBI refused to comment officially on the questioning. But an embassy source said, "The FBI wanted to hold him for questioning in relation to certain high profile assassinations in which he is suspected of playing a key role."

Toussaint also speculated he was held in the United States until three days after Sunday's senate and local elections in Haiti because he had announced his plans to run. "The Americans didn't want me in the elections," he said.

Toussaint is a former Haitian army captain who defected from the military in 1986, refusing to take part in death squad activity. He became Aristide's head of security during his 1990 presidential campaign and followed Aristide into exile in the United States after a 1991 military coup.

His attorney, Ira Kurzban, said Toussaint worked for a farmworker programme while in exile, receiving a Green Card. After U.S. troops restored Aristide in 1994, Toussaint was promoted to major and when Aristide disbanded the military in 1995 he named Toussaint interim police chief.

The United States strongly opposed that appointment, calling Toussaint a human rights violator. Early last year, the U.S. government compiled a list of former military officers loyal to Aristide who were to be denied visas for the United States.
Former Maj. Fourel Celestin, who early counts show has won a senate seat representing the Jacmel area in the south under Aristide's new Famni Lavalas party, was also on the list.
Haitian government attorneys say Toussaint wrote to the U.S. consul upon learning he was on the list explaining that he was a legal resident with a Green Card and therefore did not require a visa.
Toussaint made several trips to Miami to buy merchandise for his police and security supply store, often being detained for hours by immigration officers who questioned his papers.
